record.paper_title: Some open problems in Banach space theory
record.original_question: Let X be a Banach space that has at least two non-equivalent symmetric bases. Must X then have infinitely many mutually non-equivalent symmetric bases?

evidence.quote: X be a Banach space having at least two non equivalent symm etric bas .
Must X have infinitely many mutually non equivalent symmetric bases ?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let X be an infinite-dimensional Banach space. A Schauder basis (e_n) of X is called symmetric if for every permutation π of the positive integers, the sequence (e_{π(n)}) is also a Schauder basis of X equivalent to (e_n); equivalently, there is a constant C ≥ 1 such that for every permutation π, every choice of signs (ε_n) ∈ {−1, +1}^N, every finitely supported scalar sequence (a_n), and with the convention that only finitely many a_n are nonzero,

    C^{−1} ‖∑ a_n e_n‖ ≤ ‖∑ ε_n a_n e_{π(n)}‖ ≤ C ‖∑ a_n e_n‖.

Two Schauder bases (e_n) and (f_n) of X are called equivalent if there exist constants 0 < c ≤ C < ∞ such that for every finitely supported scalar sequence (a_n),

    c ‖∑ a_n e_n‖ ≤ ‖∑ a_n f_n‖ ≤ C ‖∑ a_n e_n‖.

Suppose X admits at least two symmetric Schauder bases that are not equivalent to each other. Must X then admit infinitely many symmetric Schauder bases that are pairwise non-equivalent?
artifact.status_search_result: The question is answered in the negative. C. J. Read constructed a Banach space possessing, up to equivalence, exactly two symmetric bases ("A Banach space with, up to equivalence, precisely two symmetric bases", Israel Journal of Mathematics, 1981). Therefore having at least two non-equivalent symmetric bases does not force the existence of infinitely many pairwise non-equivalent symmetric bases.

status_evidence.title: A Banach space with, up to equivalence, precisely two symmetric bases
status_evidence.snippet: Construction of a Banach space having exactly two non-equivalent symmetric bases.
status_evidence.claim: Provides a counterexample showing a Banach space can have exactly two non-equivalent symmetric bases, so the answer to the question is no.
